text:
Code users in the Claude Desktop app rely on folder groups, visible context, safe permission defaults and more (summary based on GitHub issues after the latest update)

After the Desktop app update that started rolling out on October 13 (2.37337.1), I had Claude read through the open GitHub issues filed about it and here's what we found about what users of Code in the Desktop app want and use, as summarized by Claude: 36 issues and their comments in the anthropics/claude-code repo. When people describe what broke, they are describing what they built their daily work around. Read together, the issues are a picture of what people actually use in Code in the Desktop app.

1. One heading per project folder, with that folder's sessions under it, in a stable order. By far the most reported. One person called it "the major reason to use the desktop app." One team reported 261 sessions across 31 project folders turning into one list. Credit where due: Anthropic replied in the main issue within a day, said "sorry for shipping this without any notice. That's on us," and shipped automatic per-folder groups by the next day. They currently appear under Group by > Environment.
2. A session list you can understand at a glance. Sessions started appearing nested under other sessions. "Nothing in the UI explains why a session shows up nested under another one."
3. How full the context window is, visible without clicking. People use it to decide when to start a fresh session: "that's how I decide when it's time to start a new session." It moved into a side panel.
4. One-click controls. The effort setting went from one click to three, and its keyboard shortcut changed.
5. Your own activity history. The stats view and the activity overview on the new-session screen were removed. People checked them daily.
6. Permission prompts where "Allow once" is the main button. "Always allow" is now the main button and "Allow once" is in a dropdown. People who work in Manual mode to review every change say this undoes that choice.
7. A conversation you can read straight through. The transcript is now split into boxes, prompt suggestions disappeared, and an end-of-turn box offers answer buttons. "For research and analysis work, the written end-of-turn report is the deliverable." I'd add the to-do checklists that now tick themselves off on every task.
8. Room for the conversation. A new right-hand panel can't be hidden, which hurts most in split view, and the "+" button moved inside the message box.
9. Scheduled task runs in the sidebar. People running from 11 to more than 50 scheduled tasks lost the sidebar section they used to open each run.
10. Knowing what changed. The Desktop changelog page is gone, there was no in-app notice, and "UI changes ship without guidance."

What this adds up to: people organized real work around specific, stable parts of the app, especially the project folder as the unit everything hangs on. These changes arrived all at once, with no notice and no way to keep the layout people already had.

What would help most, going by these threads: a changelog for Desktop app releases, notice before layout changes, and a setting to keep the current layout while trying a new one.

If something you rely on isn't here, add it in the comments. All 36 issues are linked in the first comment. That's the best place to add your support, since that's where Anthropic's desktop team is answering.

text:
Tools priced for humans who log in daily make less sense now that Claude does the logging in

A lot of the software I see people paying for was priced for a specific kind of customer: a human who logs in most days, clicks around a dashboard, exports a CSV and logs out. Monthly plans made sense for that person. They used the tool constantly, and a flat fee was easy to budget.

Claude is quietly changing who the customer is.

When Claude does the research, it doesn't need the dashboard, the seat or the saved views. It needs the data, through an API, a few times a week. Keyword volumes for one brief. A handful of pages scraped for another. An image once in a while. But the pricing hasn't caught up:
- plans with included usage you'll never get near
- credits that expire at the end of the month
- seats for something no human sits in
- minimum top-ups bigger than what Claude will spend in a quarter

The per-call price of most of these APIs is tiny. What makes them expensive for occasional use is everything wrapped around the call.

To be fair to subscriptions, they still win in two cases. If you hit one tool hard every single day, a plan is probably cheaper. And if you actually use the dashboard yourself, you're still the customer it was built for.

But for the long tail of tools Claude reaches for now and then, I think pay-per-call is the obvious model, and surprisingly few providers offer it directly without a plan attached. The ones that do tend to hide it behind an "API" tab that still asks for a monthly commitment first.

I also wonder what this does to the providers. If a big share of their usage starts coming from assistants instead of people, the dashboard stops being the product and the API becomes the product. That's a very different business.

Which tool are you still paying for monthly mainly so Claude can use it a few times?

text:
I made a Claude Code mod that shows your 5-hour and weekly limits above the prompt and warns you before you hit them

I kept getting blocked mid-week without warning, so I built two small Claude Code mods. They hook into Claude Code's plugin API, so there's no wrapper and no extra process. limits: an always-on band above the prompt 5-hour and weekly usage: a bar, the percent used and a countdown to the reset The percent turns red when your current pace would use up the limit before it resets. You find out on Tuesday, not when you're blocked on Thursday. Context window fill, plus toasts at 75/90/100%. idle-compact: cheaper returns to big chats The prompt cache expires after an hour, so coming back to a 300k-token chat reloads all of it at full price After 40 min idle, it runs /compact while the cache is still warm, so the chat you return to is small It never compacts a chat you reopened cold, since that would cost full price How it works (if you want to build your own): limits renders an AbovePrompt band from the rate-limit readings Claude Code already receives. It shares one reading across all open sessions through the plugin store, so 10 open chats still make only one 1-token Haiku request every 2 min to stay fresh. text:
Why Claude Code ignores your .claude/rules/

The model isn't actually "ignoring" the rules; it can see them in the context window. The problem is that natural language rules lack a structural trigger. Without a specific instruction telling the model when to pause and look at a rule, the model's attention drifts toward the immediate task and leaves the constraints behind. The Solution: Moving from Descriptive to Programmable Flow. To fix this, you need to move from writing "lists of instructions" to defining a "control flow." By using a syntax that utilizes labels, branches, and checks (like LNL), you create high-density attention anchors. The Comparison: the "Drift" Pattern (Natural Language), rules are static, Claude sees them but there is no "checkpoint" forcing it to stop and validate; the "Flow" Pattern (Structural Syntax) uses tags like <flow>, ASK, JUMP, CHECK, DO to force the model to constantly attend to these tokens to satisfy the structural requirements of the flow. For more details you can read my article, link in the comments.

text:
Claude Desktop on Windows stuck always-on-top after silent updates — root cause known since August, still no fix

If your Claude Desktop window on Windows stays on top of every other app, you're not alone. Cause: when the app applies a silent background update, it restores its z-order behind whatever window was above it. If that window was topmost, Claude inherits WS_EX_TOPMOST. Users diagnosed this in detail in August, with a small fix proposed. Why restarting doesn't help: closing the window and reopening just hands off to the running instance. You have to right-click the tray icon, Quit, then reopen. It comes back on the next silent update. Quick unstick without restarting, via a PowerShell script using SetWindowPos. If this affects you, upvote the GitHub issues so it gets prioritized: anthropics/claude-code issues 89467 (labeled bug) and 85891 (300+ reactions, labeled invalid). All we're asking for: fix the restore, and add a "Keep window on top" toggle in Settings, default off.

text:
Using Claude skills for multiple clients without duplicating them: how we keep client stuff out of the skills

I run an SEO agency and we've ended up with around 200 skills at this point. The thing that's made the biggest difference for us is something we've started calling "skill hooks". The problem we kept running into: a skill works pretty well, but the output's kind of generic, so you end up giving it guidance about the client's brand every time. You can put that guidance into the skill, but then the skill only works for that one client. So the rule now is that a skill only holds guidance that would work for any client. Anything client-specific lives in a doc in that client's repo, and at the step where it's needed the skill names that doc explicitly and tells the model to go read it. If the doc doesn't exist yet, the skill tells it to create it. Our article production skill has three or four of these: when it's drafting, it reads the client's brand voice doc; when it's adding internal links, it reads their internal pages doc and their competitors doc so it doesn't link to a competitor. We do the same thing for page creation, website design and video editing.

Teammates join a shared session, agree on shared interfaces, and split a ticket into tasks. Each person works from their own checkout, with their own Claude account, quota, and GitHub identity. File leases define ownership, while the shared room and live board show progress. The plugin and self-hosted server are free and open source under MIT.
